Setup (per docs/research/variance_of_associator.md § "Worked example:
single Fano generator"):
A(a, b, c) := ‖[a, b, c]‖²   where [a,b,c] = (a·b)·c − a·(b·c)
Unperturbed: [a,b,c] = 2·e_7, A = 4.

variance (from the β document, derivation):
Var(A) ≈ 64 σ²                                (TRUTH)
If the current compiler's stepwise scalar-product rule were applied
instead, it would give:
Var_compiler(A) ≈ 16 σ²                       (COMPILER, 4× low)
This test computes the sample variance of A over N = 100,000 Monte
Carlo samples and compares to the TRUTH formula. It does NOT test the
compiler's variance_of() — that requires the full Knowledge<f64>
chain which introduces unrelated complexities (see ζ buffer bug). The
compiler comparison is deferred to a separate test.
Pass criterion: |MC_var − 64σ²| / 64σ² < 0.05 (5% relative error).
If this passes, β's analytical formula is validated empirically. The
remaining claim — that the compiler produces 16σ² — is then a
separate reading-confirmation task.

Reads the committed benchmark CSV benchmarks/pbpk/model_form_uc.csv at
runtime (read_file, no embedded data) and aggregates the model-form

robust to the aggregation choice:
METHOD 1 — AUC-weighted residual fraction
Per organ:  resid1_o = |AUC28_o - AUC14_o| / AUC28_o
where AUC_o = trapezoidal integral of C_o(t) over the sample times.
Aggregate scalar (exposure-weighted across organs):
resid1 = Σ_o |AUC28_o - AUC14_o| / Σ_o AUC28_o
The 28-compartment model is the truth reference (denominator).
METHOD 2 — Peak-window residual fraction (t ≤ 6 h)
Restrict to the early/peak window where absolute exposure is highest.
Exposure-weighted (concentration-mass-weighted) relative delta:
resid2 = Σ_{t≤6h,o} |C28 - C14| / Σ_{t≤6h,o} C28
NEAR-ZERO-TAIL GUARD: the CSV's delta_pct hits 1246% at the brain
t=30h sample where C28 ≈ 1e-6. Because BOTH methods weight by absolute
exposure (AUC magnitude / concentration mass), that late-time tail is
negligible in the numerator AND denominator and CANNOT dominate. We do
NOT use the raw delta_pct column for the residual fraction.

form discrepancy, so they are NOT summed (that double-counts one source);

comments: FRONTIER (Paper 1 open item) — the exact Cayley-Dickson product over UNBOUNDED ℚ, ALL 16 components.
The i64 version (sedenion_cd_full16_q.sio) does the full 16-comp ℚ product via the common-denominator
reduction, but caps at coefficients ~1e8 (i64 output). This closes the unbounded case with a minimal,
self-contained SIGNED BigInt (base 1e9 limbs) — so numerators/denominators are ARBITRARY precision.
WHY A LOCAL BigInt. The stdlib `math::bignat` full big×big `big_mul` SIGSEGVs under souc v0.80.0
(a single `big_mul(a,b)`, no arrays, no loop — a clean #651/#637 struct-copy repro), and `[BigInt;16]`
SIGSEGVs (the array-of-structs wall). This brick CIRCUMVENTS both — it does NOT fix #651 — exactly as
the i64 common-denom circumvented #637: (i) a minimal in-file BigInt built only from primitives that
empirically compile (schoolbook big×big = big_mul_small + limb-shift + big_add-in-loop, which the spike
confirms runs); (ii) the 16 numerators are held in FLAT scalar arrays [i64;N], never [BigInt;16].
Common-denom identity: a rational sedenion = 16 integer numerators A[16] over a common denom Ad;
(A·B)[k] = (Σ_{i⊕j=k} σ(i,j) A[i] B[j]) / (Ad·Bd)  — an INTEGER 16-comp product of numerators.
Certified on two cases: (1) a known zero divisor scaled by 10^40 — product EXACTLY 0 in all 16 comps
at magnitude 10^80 (i64 would overflow into garbage; exactness holds); (2) a general 16-comp product
with unbounded rational coefficients (components up to ~10^70). Each component's residue mod 1e9+7 is
emitted (byte-identical across souc builds; a per-limb decimal printer is miscompiled differently by
bin/souc vs stage2) and cross-verified vs the Python oracle; the EXACT decimals are witnessed by Lean
(native Int, SounioCDqbig.lean) and the oracle (exact ℚ). Case 1's annihilation is checked structurally.

comments: tests/run-pass/sedenion_ratbig_channel_case1.sio
Split-out single-case variant. souc v0.80.0 hits TWO distinct codegen
flakes on the combined 3-case file, both empirically bisected here:
(a) whole-program struct-heavy function-count capacity wall (same
family as stdlib/math/bignat.sio's note) -- the combined file
(~28 fns) SIGSEGVs; trimmed to <=24 functions per file below.
(b) a SEPARATE, sharper bug: calling unat_is_zero(...) in `main` on a
BigNat pulled (directly or via a wrapper fn) out of the `.num.mag`
of a Rat that was itself produced by rat_add/rat_mul/rat_reduce
SIGSEGVs codegen every time -- even at a function count that
otherwise compiles fine, even wrapped in its own helper fn, even
as unreferenced-looking dead code. Calling unat_print (or
big_print) on the SAME value at the SAME call site is fine; only
unat_is_zero (or an inlined equivalent boolean field compare) on
that specific derivation chain crashes. Root cause not
determined (register/stack-slot corruption is suspected given the
deep gcd/divmod call tree inside rat_reduce, but not confirmed).
WORKAROUND: do not call any is-zero check on a rat_add/rat_mul
result inside the .sio at all -- print the reduced (num, den)
pair (rat_print) and decide zero-ness FROM THE PRINTED OUTPUT
(canonical reduced form means num=0,den=1 iff the value is
exactly zero). That is exactly the "decidable rational equality"
the task asks for, so no functionality is lost.
(c) a THIRD, real correctness bug (not just a crash): souc's by-value
struct-copy semantics are violated by the "var r = a; r.neg =
!a.neg; ...; r" pattern this file's big_neg originally used
(copied verbatim from stdlib/math/bignat.sio) -- mutating r.neg

place when computing delta = -s, so later reuses of `s` picked up
the flipped sign. FIXED by rewriting big_neg to build a fresh
a fresh BigInt struct literal (mag unchanged, neg flipped) instead of
copy-then-mutate; this stdlib/math/bignat.sio big_neg pattern
should be treated as suspect anywhere it is reused. Do NOT trust
"compiles and runs and prints a plausible-looking number" here --

The signed domain gave Sub an escape hatch: a non-disjoint pair is ALLOWED
when ns_cov_nonneg proves every shared source carries a non-negative
coefficient product. That certificate is only as good as the signs feeding
it, and the transfer originally sent every operator except Sub, Mul and Div

r = a % b        published a's and b's additive signs as if they were r's

and COMPILED
but Rem's Jacobian signs are not the additive join of its operands' signs, so
that certificate was unfounded and Var(r - a) could be understated -- the
exact thing E230 exists to refuse, reintroduced through the new escape hatch
rather than through the rule it guards.
The fix makes ns_union_opaque the DEFAULT and ns_union the exception (OpAdd
only): an operator nobody has modelled marks its result sign-unknown, and
ns_cov_nonneg fails closed on it. This file must stay refused. If it ever
compiles again, the transfer has gone back to trusting signs it cannot derive.

comments: refinement_subtype_strict
The pattern used to read E001, which this program never emits — it is rejected
by the refinement checker with an uncoded diagnostic. The harness was not
matching error-pattern at all, so the test passed while asserting the wrong
thing; with the matcher fixed the annotation had to say what is actually
emitted.
`requires: lean_single` because the diagnostic this asserts is an engine
difference, not a language rule. Measured 2026-09-03 on both:
lean_single  error[E208]: refinement type violation — value 0 does not
satisfy parameter predicate at line 19        ← what is asserted
Madaros      error[E008] return value does not match declared return type
error[E001] this binding expects a different type
error[E009] argument type does not match parameter
Madaros is not missing the diagnostic — check.sio carries code 42, "value does
not satisfy the refinement predicate". It never reaches it, because it relates
a refinement type to its base type in NEITHER direction:
fn f(x: Positive) -> i32 { x }    E008, though every Positive IS an i32
let p: Positive = 0               E001, a bare type mismatch standing where
the predicate should have spoken
So the three errors above are all one gap wearing three codes, and the E009 at
the call site rejects for the wrong reason: NonNeg and Positive differ as
NAMES, not because 0 fails `n > 0`. Two identical refinement names with a
violated predicate would slip through it.
Erasure (Positive → i32) would be sound to open on its own. The introduction
direction is where the predicate must actually be evaluated, and opening it
without first proving the check fires would turn a wrongly-coded rejection
into an acceptance — a fail-open in a type system. Left for whoever implements
refinement subsumption in the modular checker, rather than half-done here.
